title: Chapter XLIV

teacherSummary.text: Darcy brings Georgiana and Bingley to meet Elizabeth. Georgiana is shy, not proud. Bingley seems to remember Jane. The Gardiners notice Darcy's affection.

vocabulary.definition: A quality of bodies which corrodes or destroys others
vocabulary.context: Gratitude, not merely for having once loved her, but for loving her still well enough, to forgive all the petulance and acrimony of her manner in rejecting him, and all the unjust accusations accompanying her rejection.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “acrimony”: ac- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: She found it difficult to obtain even a word from her beyond a monosyllable.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “monosyllable”: mono- (Greek monos, "single") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To bestow a share or portion of
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth immediately recognising the livery, guessed what it meant, and imparted no small degree of surprise to her relations, by acquainting them with the honour which she expected.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “impart”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of retiring or withdrawing one's self, especially from what is dangerous or disagreeable
vocabulary.context: She retreated from the window, fearful of being seen; and as she walked up and down the room, endeavouring to compose herself, saw such looks of enquiring surprise in her uncle and aunt, as made everything worse.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “retreat”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To form by putting together two or more things or parts
vocabulary.context: She retreated from the window, fearful of being seen; and as she walked up and down the room, endeavouring to compose herself, saw such looks of enquiring surprise in her uncle and aunt, as made everything worse.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “compose”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act, practice, or art of one who fishes
vocabulary.context: The fishing scheme had been renewed the day before, and a positive engagement made of his meeting some of the gentlemen at Pemberley by noon.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fishing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Miss Darcy and her brother appeared, and this formidable introduction took place.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “formidable”: form (Latin forma, "shape") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: The suspicions which had just arisen of Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “suspicion”: spic (Latin specere, "to look"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Miss Darcy was tall, and on a larger scale than Elizabeth; and, though little more than sixteen, her figure was formed, and her appearance womanly and graceful.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “sixteen”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To hinder from freedom of thought, speech, or action by something which impedes or confuses mental action
vocabulary.context: With astonishment did Elizabeth see, that her new acquaintance was at least as much embarrassed as herself.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “embarrass”: em- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Introducing a sister was a sign of serious intentions.

significance: Darcy's courtesy to the Gardiners proves he has changed.
discussionQuestions: What evidence shows Darcy has changed?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

items.prompt: Whom does Darcy introduce to Elizabeth?
Who seems to remember Jane fondly?
How does Darcy treat the Gardiners?

In the line “Gratitude, not merely for having once loved her, but for loving her still well enough, to forgive all the petulance and acrimony of her manner in rejecting him, and all the unjust accusations accompanying her rejection.”, what does “acrimony” most nearly mean?
options: To bestow a share or portion of
The act of retiring or withdrawing one's self, especially from what is dangerous or disagreeable
A quality of bodies which corrodes or destroys others

items.prompt: In the line “She found it difficult to obtain even a word from her beyond a monosyllable.”, what does “monosyllable” most nearly mean?

answerKey.answer: A quality of bodies which corrodes or destroys others

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XLIV,” how does Austen show a changed Darcy? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XLIV develops the idea of a changed Darcy. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XLIV to complicate the reader's understanding of a changed Darcy. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XLIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a changed Darcy responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XLIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a changed Darcy. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: Miss Darcy and her brother appeared, and this formidable introduction took place. With astonishment did Elizabeth see, that her new acquaintance was at least as much embarrassed as herself. Since her being at Lambton, she had heard that Miss Darcy was exceedingly proud; but the observation of a very few minutes convinced her, that she was only exceedingly shy. She found it difficult to obtain even a word from her beyond a monosyllable.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XLIV”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: Miss Darcy and her brother appeared, and this formidable introduction took place. With astonishment did Elizabeth see, that her new acquaintance was at least as much embarrassed as herself. Since her being at Lambton, she had heard that Miss Darcy was exceedingly proud; but the observation of a very few minutes convinced her, that she was only exceedingly shy. She found it difficult to obtain even a word from her beyond a monosyllable.

annotationFocus.label: Theme
annotationFocus.lookFor: statements or moments that connect to the book's big ideas

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What evidence shows Darcy has changed? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are acrimony, monosyllable, imparted, retreated, compose. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Gratitude, not merely for having once loved her, but for loving her still well enough, to forgive all the petulance and acrimony of her manner in rejecting him, and all the unjust accusations accompanying her rejection.” Webster's says: A quality of bodies which corrodes or destroys others. Now the word history: “acrimony”: ac- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “monosyllable”: mono- (Greek monos, "single") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “impart”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Introducing a sister was a sign of serious intentions. Why does this chapter matter? Darcy's courtesy to the Gardiners proves he has changed. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a changed Darcy.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

Since her being at Lambton, she had heard that Miss Darcy was exceedingly proud; but the observation of a very few minutes convinced her, that she was only exceedingly shy. She found it difficult to obtain even a word from her beyond a monosyllable.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Theme, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XLIV,” how does Austen show a changed Darcy? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a changed Darcy, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes a changed Darcy. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
